Reaching LDL-c targets in high-risk patients requires high-efﬁcacy
cholesterol-lowering drugs in more than 50% of cases.
The results of the CHECK study夽
Andrea Poli a,∗ , Manuela Casula a , Elena Tragni a , Ovidio Brignoli b , Alessandro Filippi b ,
Claudio Cricelli b , Alberico L. Catapano a
a

a b s t r a c t
We estimated the need to use low-efﬁcacy statins or high-efﬁcacy statins or drug combinations to bring
high- or very-high cardiovascular risk subjects to their LDL-c target, in a sample representative of the
Italian adult population and according to the principles of reimbursement of hypercholesterolemic drugs
currently used in Italy. The results allow us concluding that among high or very high cardiovascular risk
patients about three patients out of ﬁve should be prescribed high-efﬁcacy statins or drug combinations.
The other two prescriptions might take into account lower-efﬁcacy statins.
If we also compute the values of HDL-c in these subjects – the large majority of which stands below
the optimal values as suggested by International guidelines – we bring forward the need either to select
speciﬁc statins able to increase the levels of these protective lipoproteins or to consider combination
therapies of statins with ﬁbrates or nicotinic acid.
Our data might conceivably be applied to other low-cardiovascular risk countries and should be taken
into account when deﬁning the proportion of drugs with different efﬁcacy and cost in the everyday
clinical practice.

1. Introduction
The control of plasma low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDLc) concentrations is a pillar of cardiovascular prevention [1,2]. The
results of controlled clinical intervention trials showed the existence of a linear correlation (1%:1%) between the reduction of LDL-c
induced by treatments and the reduction of the relative risk of
coronary events in treated subjects [3].
Since the early ‘90s, International guidelines have set out the
basic criteria for the clinical management of hypocholesterolemic
treatments. Such guidelines identify speciﬁc therapeutic targets
(target levels) for LDL-c, to be adopted in clinical practice. Target
levels decrease along with the increase in global cardiovascular risk. In the US guidelines, such values ﬂuctuate within a
wide range, i.e. from 70 mg/dL for subjects at very high cardiovascular risk to 160 mg/dL for subject at very low risk [4].

The range of LDL-c targets in the European guidelines is narrower, spanning from 80 to 115 mg/dL [5]. Bringing a patient
to his/her LDL-c target is likely to be the most important criterion to deﬁne the clinical appropriateness of his/her lipid proﬁle
management.
It appears quite clear that reaching the therapeutic target
requires the adoption of different strategies, depending on the gap
between the basal and the desired LDL-c target levels. Drugs which
are more or less efﬁcacious should, in fact, be speciﬁcally employed
based on such gap.
The most effective (in terms of plasma LDL cholesterol reducing
capacity) drugs, e.g. atorvastatin and rosuvastatin [6], are currently more expensive than the older, less efﬁcacious statins (now
available as generic); therefore it appears necessary to identify
appropriate criteria of selection of the different available hypolipidemic drugs, to optimize their use and help to control current
expenditure.
Information on the relative distribution of subjects’ risk levels
in populations is still scanty. Consequently, we lack solid data on
the distribution of the corresponding target levels for LDL-c in the
population. Recently, using data from the CHECK study, we deﬁned
the distribution of LDL-c targets and the individual distance from

target in a sample of about 5500 subjects, representative of the
Italian adult population [7].
The aim of the current analysis was to deﬁne the number of
subjects who could reach their therapeutic target using statins of
moderate efﬁcacy or, rather, using high-potency, more expensive
statins (or hypolipidemic drugs combinations) in a representative
sample of the Italian adult population. For practical reasons we have
limited our analyses to high- or very high-cardiovascular risk subjects, for whom the Italian National health system refunds statins
prescription, in accordance to available evidence and published
guidelines [8].
Recently, much attention has also being paid to the plasma levels
of the cholesterol fraction bound to high density lipoproteins (HDLc) as a key component of global risk. In particular, low HDL-c plasma
levels are the target of speciﬁc treatments, according to some guidelines, in subjects who are already being adequately treated for
elevated LDL-c. Such interventions might in fact tackle the so-called
“residual risk”, recorded in clinical trials where LDL-c had been
normalized [9]. Accordingly, in this study we have calculated the
distribution of HDL-c in the high- or very high cardiovascular risk
subjects of the cohort and the distance between their current and
optimal HDL-c values, in order to identify subjects who would theoretically need pharmacological treatment aimed at concomitantly
ameliorate both LDL- and HDL-c plasma levels.
2. Patients and methods
The protocol of the CHECK study has been fully described elsewhere [7]. In brief, 425 general practitioners who participated in
the study randomly extracted – from their patients’ databases –
16 subjects between 40 and 79 years of age. Each component of
the cohort obtained with this procedure (n = 5846) went through a
complete clinical and anamnestic evaluation by his/her physician.
A blood sample was drawn after an overnight fast and a central laboratory (Fleming spa, Brescia, Italy) assessed the main biochemical
markers of cardiovascular risk, namely plasma total cholesterol,
LDL-c, and HDL-c, triglycerides, apoB, and glucose. The population recruited in the CHECK study exhibited a distribution of age
and of the main anthropometric and cardiovascular risk indices
in good accordance with those published by the National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT) for the Italian adult population, and by
other national cohorts, thus conﬁrming the appropriateness of the
randomization procedure and of the sample extraction from the
databases.
For each component of the cohort, we calculated the level of
global cardiovascular risk through a combination of clinical data
(presence of cardiovascular disease or diabetes) and the use, when
appropriate, of an algorithm developed by the Italian National
Institute of Health (Istituto Superiore di Sanità, ISS) to evaluate
cardiovascular risk in the Italian population [10]. The appropriate
target for LDL-c was then deﬁned, for each component of the cohort,
based on criteria shown in Table 1,
From hereafter, analyses was limited to high- or very-high cardiovascular risk subjects; for each of these subjects we estimated
the distance, as percentage, between the basal LDL-c and the target
values, according to the following formula:
Distance from target (DFT) = [(observed LDL-c − target LDLc)/observed LDL-c] × 100. DFTs were then clustered in 2.5% groups.
Subjects who were not under statin treatment at enrollment
in the CHECK cohort were then subdivided into groups that
would beneﬁt from different hypocholesterolemic treatments, as
follows:
• Subjects with DFT <20% were allocated to the “diet, soluble ﬁber,
soy protein, and phytosterols” group, based on the maximal

• Subjects with DFT between 20% and 37.5% were allocated to
the “standard efﬁcacy statin” group, based on the average LDL-c
reducing efﬁcacy of simvastatin (the generic statin with the best
cost/efﬁcacy ratio) at a dosage of 40 mg/day. The 80 mg/day dose
of this molecule has a suboptimal efﬁcacy/safety ratio [12].
• The remaining subjects, with DFT >37.5%, were allocated to the
“high efﬁcacy treatment” group (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin + ezetimibe association).
Subjects who were treated with statins at enrollment and who
were already “at target” (or were <7.5% from it) were allocated
half in the “standard efﬁcacy statin” group and half in the “high
efﬁcacy treatment” group, based on the respective approximate
market share of these two groups of drugs in Italy.
Patients with a DFT ≥7.5% treated with a statin at enrollment
were allocated to the “high efﬁcacy treatment” group. We did
this because we hypothesized that: (a) dietetic interventions had
already been proposed by the primary care physician before the
statin treatment; hence, this kind of intervention would not further
exert any remarkable effect in these patients and (b) even doubling
the dose of the adopted statin would not, on average, allow to reach
the target, according to statin drugs pharmacology [13].
Similar calculations were performed to identify the number of
patients in need of an intervention yielding a 45% or a 50% LDL-c
reduction to reach their LDL-c target.
The patients of the cohort were also classiﬁed “at-target” or
“not-at-target” for HDL-c levels, by using, as reference values, HDLc >40 mg/dL for males and >50 mg/dL for females. Their individual
distance from their HDL-c target has been estimated and analyzed
with computations similar to those used for LDL-c.
3. Results
Among the CHECK subjects of whom all clinical and biochemical
relevant data were available (n = 5456), 1325 subjects were classiﬁed at high or very high risk. 21% of them were treated with a statin
at enrolment.
81% of these high or very high risk patients were “not-at-target”;
more speciﬁcally, 84% of non-statin-treated patients, and 73% of
statin treated patients, were “not-at-target”.
Based on the criteria outlined above, 13% of these high or
very high risk patients need no treatment, being already “attarget”; 24% of the sample needs a non-pharmacological treatment
(diet, ﬁber, soy, phytosterols) to reach their target, 29% need a
standard-efﬁcacy statin, and 34% need a high-efﬁcacy hypolipidemic treatment.

These percentages have been transposed upon an age equivalent Italian population segment (40–79 years old; n = 29 millions).
To also include in the ﬁnal assessment subjects younger than 40
years, we added to the estimate of the number of candidates to
high-efﬁcacy treatment the number of subjects, younger than 40
years, who carry genetic dyslipidemia, whose distance from their
LDL-c target would largely exceed 37.5%. The total number of these
patients has been estimated to be 250,000, hypothesizing a 0.2%
prevalence of familial hypercholesterolemia and a 1% prevalence
of combined familial dyslipidemia, limiting treatment indication
to subjects older than 18 years.
Conversely, we considered as not relevant the prevalence of a
high cardiovascular risk condition among subjects younger than
40 years, because of the very limited number of subjects – in this
age frame – with frank cardiovascular disease and/or with a global
cardiovascular risk at 10 years ≥20% according to the risk algorithm
we used.
With these assumptions, we estimated the distribution of
classes of DFT – as shown in Table 2 – and calculated the absolute
number of patients (in Italy) candidate to the use of the different
hypocholesterolemic strategies outlined above. The optimal proportion of standard statins or high-efﬁcacy drugs would be 43%
and 57% of total prescription of hypocholesterolemic drugs, respectively.
With similar calculations, it is possible to estimate the absolute
numbers of Italian patients who would need, to reach their LDLc target, a hypocholesterolemic treatment able to decrease LDL-c
levels by, at least, 45% or 50%, respectively. Figures are presented

4. Discussion
While only one third of the total CHECK cohort and, in turn, of
the total adult Italian population, is “not-at-target” for LDL-c [8],
among the high- or very high cardiovascular risk subject analyzed
in this article this percentage markedly increases and approaches
90%. This difference is largely explained by the noticeably lower
LDL-c target values established for those subjects by the lipid management guidelines.
The appropriate use – in cardiovascular prevention – of highefﬁcacy statins (currently still covered by a patent and, thus, more
expensive) or of cheaper statins (whose patent expired) is still the
subject of a heated debate. According to the major International
Guidelines, increasing cardiovascular risk calls for lower LDL-c targets; thus, the choice of a speciﬁc hypocholesterolemic drug needs
to take into account its efﬁcacy in reducing LDL-c and the DFT of
the subject to be treated.
Our data demonstrate that, in Italy, high- and very-high risk
subjects need to use a higher proportion of high-efﬁcacy drugs
as compared to the standard-efﬁcacy ones to reach as an average their therapeutic targets. In brief, 2.68 million patients would
need high-efﬁcacy treatments vs. 2.05 millions that would need the
standard ones (57% vs. 43%, respectively). Conversely (especially
among medium- or low-risk subjects), a very high number of subjects could reach their LDL-c therapeutic targets simply adopting
non-pharmacological therapies, based on an appropriate consumption of dietary fats, soluble ﬁber, phytosterols, and soy protein.
Notably, this non-pharmacological approach does not bring about
direct costs to the National Health care system.
In practice, the simplest approach to the use of a high-efﬁcacy
statin would be the identiﬁcation of a DFT, as assessed by the
(observed LDL-c-target LDL-c)/observed LDL-c formula, higher than
37.5% after an appropriate dietary test.
Within this frame, the ability of some statins – or of other
hypocholesterolemic drugs – to increase HDL-c will gain considerable interest. Even though pharmacological correction of HDL-c
is not thought – to date – to provide the same degree of protection afforded by LDL-c reduction, evidence is available suggesting
that increasing HDL-c is associated with a reduction of cardiovascular risk and to a slower evolution of already-formed atheromas
[14,15].
In the CHECK cohort we examined, the large majority of subjects at high or very high cardiovascular risk do not feature optimal
levels of HDL-c. Most of these patients have HDL-c values which
are at least 10% lower than optimal values (>40 mg/dL for men and
>50 mg/dL for women). In these patients, the use of drugs with speciﬁc actions on this parameter might contribute to further reducing
their cardiovascular risk.

5. Conclusions
We estimated the need to use low-efﬁcacy statins or highefﬁcacy statins or drug combinations to bring high- or very-high
cardiovascular risk subjects to their LDL-c target, in a sample representative of the Italian adult population and according to the
principles of reimbursement of hypercholesterolemic drugs currently used in Italy. The results allow us concluding that among
high or very high cardiovascular risk patients about three patients
out of ﬁve should be prescribed high-efﬁcacy statins or drug combinations. The other two prescriptions might take into account
lower-efﬁcacy statins.
If we also compute the values of HDL-c in these subjects – the
large majority of which stands below the optimal values as suggested by International guidelines – we bring forward the need
either to select speciﬁc statins able to increase the levels of these
protective lipoproteins or to consider combination therapies of
statins with ﬁbrates or nicotinic acid.
Our data might conceivably be applied to other lowcardiovascular risk countries and should be taken into account
when deﬁning the proportion of drugs with different efﬁcacy and
cost in the everyday clinical practice.
